x_to_y: This edge represents a causal effect of \(x\) on \(y\): changing \(x\) (through some policy, treatment, or decision variable) shifts the outcome \(y\), holding other relevant determinants fixed. The main threats are omitted confounding (variables that affect both \(x\) and \(y\)), reverse causality if \(y\) also feeds back into \(x\), and selection or measurement error that makes variation in \(x\) non-comparable across units. Next, the researcher should clarify the source of identifying variation in \(x\) (e.g., randomized assignment, IV, panel with fixed effects, DiD) and assess balance/pre-trends or placebo tests that would support the claim that \(x\) is as-good-as-random with respect to unobserved drivers of \(y\).
y_to_z: This edge means changes in \(y\) cause changes in \(z\), capturing a direct economic channel from the outcome or policy variable \(y\) into the downstream variable \(z\) (e.g., demand shifting prices, or income affecting consumption). The main risks are omitted common causes of \(y\) and \(z\) (confounding), reverse causality if \(z\) also affects \(y\), and measurement error in \(y\) that can attenuate or distort the estimated causal effect. Next, a researcher should articulate the specific mechanism linking \(y\) to \(z\) and assess identification by checking balance/parallel trends or instrument validity (as applicable), plus sensitivity to adding plausible confounders and testing for feedback from \(z\) to \(y\).
